salt_presence.description: Indicates whether salt is present (true) or not (false) in the water.

message.content:
The ocean’s hue isn’t fixed—it shifts with light, depth, clarity, and what’s floating in it—but most people think of “blue” as its classic look:

| Factor | Typical Effect |
|--------|----------------|
| **Depth** | Shallow waters scatter more green‑yellow wavelengths, giving a turquoise/greenish tint. In deeper zones, red and orange light get absorbed first, leaving only short‑wavelength blues visible—hence the deep navy or indigo seen far offshore. |
| **Angle & Sunlight** | At sunrise/sunset the sun’s lower path lets longer wavelengths reach us, turning the surface into golden or pinkish hues. Overhead noon sunlight gives a crisp, bright blue. |
| **Clarity / Particles** | Clear, clean seas reflect sky color strongly → vivid azure. Turbid or algae‑rich waters absorb more reds and yellows, so they appear greener or even brownish. |
| **Salt & Organic Matter** | Saltwater itself doesn’t change color much, but dissolved minerals and plankton give subtle variations—from pale teal near reefs to murky olive where phytoplankton blooms occur. |

So while we often picture the sea as a single shade of blue, it actually spans a spectrum from emerald greens off coastlines to midnight indigos at great depths—all shaped by physics, biology, and weather!
